nodes.label: Charitable Trusts
nodes.summary: The four heads of charity (Pemsel classification), public benefit requirement, exclusive charitability, cy-pres doctrine, and parens patriae jurisdiction.

nodes.label: The Four Heads of Charity (Pemsel Classification)
nodes.summary: Trusts for purposes within the spirit of the preamble to the Statute of Charitable Uses 1601: relief of poverty, advancement of education, advancement of religion, and other purposes beneficial to the community. Must be exclusively charitable.

nodes.label: Public Benefit Requirement
nodes.summary: Charitable trusts must benefit the public or a sufficient section of the community. Poverty trusts have a more generous public benefit test. Beneficiaries must not be a private class.

nodes.label: Exclusive Charitability
nodes.summary: A trust must be exclusively charitable. No private purpose or personal benefit to individuals. Even a slight private interest may defeat exclusive charitability.

nodes.label: Cy-pres Doctrine
nodes.summary: Where a charitable purpose becomes impossible, impractical, or has been fulfilled, the court may apply the funds cy-pres (as near as possible) to the original purpose, provided a general charitable intention is found.

nodes.label: Parens Patriae Jurisdiction
nodes.summary: The Secretary for Justice acts as parens patriae to enforce charitable trusts. The court has supervisory jurisdiction over charitable trusts and may direct administrative schemes.

nodes.label: Gilmour v Coats [1949] AC 426
nodes.summary: Public benefit: cloistered nuns failed public benefit test because their secluded life provided no demonstrable benefit to the public.

nodes.label: Dingle v Turner [1972] AC 601
nodes.summary: Public benefit: poverty trusts may have a more generous test; trust for poor employees of a company may be charitable if not limited to named individuals.

nodes.label: To Kan Chi v Pui Man Yau (Tsing Shan Monastery) [1995] 2 HKLR 22 (CA)
nodes.summary: Exclusive charitability: temple not charitable because privately owned by the To Clan; even slight private interest defeats exclusive charitability.

nodes.label: Secretary for Justice v Joseph Lo Kin Ching [2001] 4 HKCFAR 1
nodes.summary: Cy-pres / parens patriae: CFA directed an administrative scheme to fulfil Nina Kung's charitable will, establishing a supervising body for a Nobel-level Chinese prize.

nodes.label: Verify HK Charitable Trust Cases
nodes.summary: Research HK statutory regulation of charities, Inland Revenue Ordinance charitable exemption provisions, and HK court decisions on cy-pres and public benefit.
